what_its_for: Chlorambucil is a chemotherapy medicine used to treat certain types of cancer, including chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), Hodgkin's lymphoma, and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. It works by slowing or stopping the growth of cancer cells in your body.
how_to_take: Take chlorambucil by mouth, exactly as your doctor tells you. You can take it with or without food, but taking it on an empty stomach (at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal) may help your body absorb it better. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Do not crush, break, or chew the tablet. Wash your hands thoroughly before and after handling this medicine. Try to take it at the same time each day to help you remember.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your body size, the type of cancer being treated, and how well your kidneys and liver are working. Doses can vary widely, and your doctor may adjust your dose based on blood test results. Never change your dose or stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day. If you do not remember until the next day, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do NOT take two doses on the same day to make up for a missed one. Call your doctor or pharmacist if you are unsure what to do.
storage: Store chlorambucil in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Keep it in its original container, away from light and moisture. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet. Ask your pharmacist or doctor about the safest way to dispose of any leftover medicine through a take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Avoid contact with people who have active infections, colds, flu, or contagious illnesses, because this medicine weakens your immune system. Do not receive any live vaccines (such as the nasal flu vaccine or shingles vaccine) while taking chlorambucil without talking to your doctor first. Avoid becoming pregnant or fathering a child during treatment, as this medicine can cause serious harm to an unborn baby. Use reliable birth control during treatment and for some time after. Avoid breastfeeding while on this medicine. Limit alcohol use as it may increase the risk of side effects. Avoid handling crushed or broken tablets — if you accidentally touch a broken tablet, wash the area with soap and water right away.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience any of the following: fever (temperature above 100.4°F or 38°C), chills, or signs of infection; unusual bruising or bleeding; severe skin rash, blistering, or peeling; trouble breathing or shortness of breath; yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice); seizures or tremors; extreme tiredness or weakness; mouth sores that make it hard to eat or drink; blood in your urine or stools; swollen lymph nodes that are new or getting bigger; or signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing.
when_it_works: Chlorambucil works gradually over time. Some people begin to see improvements in their blood counts or symptoms within a few weeks, but it may take several months of treatment to see the full benefit. Your doctor will monitor your progress with regular blood tests. Do not stop taking the medicine even if you feel well, unless your doctor tells you to.
special_populations: Pregnancy: This medicine can cause serious birth defects or harm to an unborn baby. Both men and women should use effective birth control during treatment and discuss this with their doctor. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed while taking chlorambucil, as it may pass into breast milk and harm the baby. Children: Chlorambucil can be used in children under careful medical supervision, but it may affect growth and development. Older adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects, especially low blood counts and infections, and may need closer monitoring. Kidney or liver problems: If you have kidney or liver disease, your doctor may need to adjust your dose or monitor you more closely.
